lead: The logical design of an IoT system lists the jobs it must do — identify, sense, act, process, communicate, serve, manage and secure — without saying which chip, board or radio does them. It exists so a design can be argued, costed and compared before any hardware is bought, and so a system built in 2015 can be checked against one built today. Engineers use it as a checklist, buyers use it to compare two products that look identical on the shelf.
prereq: You need: 1.1 for what makes a thing an IoT thing, and 1.2 for the physical parts that carry out these functions.

sections.h3: Two designs of the same system

blocks.text: The physical design names the parts you can hold: sensor, control unit, radio module, battery. The logical design names the jobs the system must do. The same jobs appear whether the radio is Wi-Fi, LoRa or a wire, and whether the processor is a low-cost microcontroller or a cloud server.

This separation exists because hardware ages fast and functions do not. A cold-chain monitoring system built years ago and one built today share almost no parts. Both identify their boxes, sense temperature, decide whether it is too warm, move the reading to a server and raise an alert. Designing at the level of functions lets a review ask whether every necessary job is covered, before anyone buys a board.
Some syllabi call this the logical design, some the functional view, and some simply IoT functional blocks. All three mean the same thing.

A functional block is a job, not a part. One device often does several blocks at once: a sensor node identifies itself, senses, filters and transmits. One block often spans many devices: the service block may run on three servers. Treat each block as a question the system must answer, and the hardware as one possible answer. The layers that organise where these blocks sit are covered in 1.5.
Two blocks are not in the main line of flow: management and security act on the others. Keep them in the list. Dropping them is the most common design error.

items: Identification gives every thing a name and an address. The name (a serial number, an EPC, a UUID) says which thing it is; the address (an IP address or a URI) says where to reach it.
Sensing collects the state of the thing or its surroundings: temperature in °C, a GPS fix, a door open or closed.
Actuation changes the physical world: a relay starts a compressor, a valve opens, a buzzer sounds. It is sensing in reverse.
Processing turns raw readings into meaning: average ten samples, drop a spike, compare with a limit of 8 °C, decide "excursion".
Communication moves data from the place it is produced to the place it is used.
Services present useful output: an alert on a phone, a dashboard, a reply from an API, a line in a billing system.
Management keeps the system running: set the sampling interval, push new firmware, detect a sensor that has gone silent, log battery level.
Security protects all of the above: prove a device is genuine, encrypt the link, decide who may read the data.

blocks.text: Processing is not tied to one place. A first pass often runs on the device, close to the sensor, to cut noise and traffic. A second pass runs on a server, where data from many devices is combined. Same block, two locations. That choice is an engineering trade-off, not a change of design.
Protocols, boards and radios are deliberately left out of this list. They are the implementation. The protocols that carry the communication block are in Unit 3, and actuator hardware is in Unit 2.

sections.h3: The path from thing to service

blocks.text: The blocks are not a random list. They describe one path that data follows, and that path is what the figure below draws.

items: Identify — the device presents its name and address when it joins the network.
Sense — the sensor produces a value with a unit and a timestamp.
Process (first pass) — filter, average, convert units, discard readings that have not changed.
Communicate — move the payload over the network.
Process (second pass) — combine with other devices, compare against a model, decide.
Serve — send an alert, update a dashboard, write a row to a database.

blocks.text: Actuation is not a step after services. It is a return path from the decision back to the physical device: when processing decides, the act block drives an actuator at the device end, for example the cooling unit restarts. The service block can inform a person at the same time.

blocks.where: D is the number of data items produced per day; N is the number of data-producing sources; T is the sampling interval in seconds; 86400 is the number of seconds in one day. This formula assumes every source produces exactly one data item every T seconds and that all sources share the same interval T.

blocks.text: Management sets T and then checks that D items actually arrive; a device whose count falls to zero has failed. Security applies to every block, with particular attention to identification, communication, services and management, because those are places where a stranger can interfere. Both act across the path rather than inside it.

figure.caption: The cold-chain van's path: 9 sources sample every 300 s, giving 2,592 data items a day. Processing compares 9 °C with the 8 °C limit, sends the phone alert through services, and drives the cooling unit back via actuation; management sets the interval and security guards every block.

spec.title: Cold-chain van: blocks and path
spec.aria: A downward cold-chain path runs from identification to sensing, processing, communication and services, with processing comparing 9 °C against an 8 °C limit; actuation returns from processing to restart cooling, while management sets T=300 s and security guards every block.

examples.question: A cold-chain van carries 6 temperature sensors, 1 GPS unit and 2 door sensors. Each sensor produces one data item every 5 minutes. Find the total number of data items the van produces per day, and name the functional block that decides a reading of 9 °C needs an alert.
steps: Count the data-producing sources: N = 6 temperature + 1 GPS + 2 door = 9 sources.
Convert the sampling interval to seconds: T = 5 minutes = 5 × 60 = 300 s.
Samples per source per day = 86400 ÷ T = 86400 ÷ 300 = 288 samples.
Data items per day D = N × 288 = 9 × 288 = 2592 data items.
The processing block compares 9 °C with the 8 °C limit and decides on the alert. The services block then presents it to a person.
examples.answer: The van produces 2,592 data items per day, and the processing block makes the alert decision.
examples.check:
sources = 6 + 1 + 2
interval_s = 5 * 60
samples = 86400 // interval_s
print(sources)
print(samples)
print(sources * samples)

examples.question: A shop installs 3 door sensors and 2 temperature sensors. Every sensor sends one reading every 30 seconds. How many data items reach the server in one day?

traps: Asked for functional blocks, do not answer Arduino, Raspberry Pi, Wi-Fi or MQTT. Functions are verbs: identify, sense, act, process, communicate, serve, manage, secure.
Identification is not only addressing. A name says which thing it is; an address says where to reach it. The one block covers both, and neither replaces the other.
Do not merge processing with services. Deciding that 9 °C is too warm is processing; showing that decision on a phone is a service.
Management and security are blocks, not afterthoughts. A question asking which block is missing usually wants one of these two.
Unit slip: 5 minutes is 300 s, not 50 s. Convert the interval to seconds before dividing into 86400.

quiz.q: Name six functional blocks of an IoT system.
quiz.a: Any six of: identification, sensing, actuation, communication, processing, services, management, security.

quiz.q: Why is a functional block described as a verb and not as a noun?
quiz.a: A block names a job the system must do, such as sense or decide. The noun is the device that does the job, and the device may change without changing the job.

quiz.q: One microcontroller board senses, filters and transmits. Does that break the block model?
quiz.a: No. A block is a function, not a part. One device may carry several blocks, just as one block may be spread over several devices.

quiz.q: A warehouse has 3 door sensors and 2 temperature sensors, each sampling every 30 seconds. Find the number of data items per day.
quiz.a: N = 3 + 2 = 5. T = 30 s, so samples per source per day = 86400 ÷ 30 = 2880. D = 5 × 2880 = 14,400 data items per day.

quiz.q: A reading of 9 °C arrives against a stored limit of 8 °C, and an alert appears on a phone. Name the blocks involved, in order.
quiz.a: Sensing produces the reading; processing compares it with the limit and decides; communication carries the result; services present the alert on the phone. Security protects the transfer.

quiz.q: A team replaces a Wi-Fi module with NB-IoT and moves filtering from the device to the cloud. Which parts of the logical design change?
quiz.a: The communication block is implemented differently and the processing block moves location. The list of blocks itself is unchanged, which is the purpose of a logical design: it stays valid while the hardware and the placement of work change.

quiz.q: Why is security drawn as a block that touches all others instead of a step after services?
quiz.a: Every block carries its own risk. Identification can be spoofed, communication can be intercepted, services can be reached by the wrong user, and management commands can be forged. A single step at the end would leave the earlier blocks unprotected.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry teams use this functional list as a requirements checklist at the start of a project and as a fault-hunting map later, when one block misbehaves. Researchers argue about where the split between on-device processing and server processing should fall, which is the edge-versus-cloud question. Reference architectures from standards bodies group the same functions under different names, so read them by function, not by label. Useful search terms: IoT reference model functional groups, edge computing offload, digital twin functional view.
